story: Many people believe the Moon changes shape because the Earth’s shadow falls across it. That’s a myth. Unless there’s a lunar eclipse, the shadow you see is actually the Moon’s own night side. We see phases because the Moon constantly orbits us, and our perspective of its sunlit half shifts daily. Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun, even during a 'New Moon' when it's simply facing away from us. This cycle is so predictable that ancient humans in Scotland built the world’s oldest known calendar to track it 10,000 years ago—5,000 years before the Mesopotamians. We also get a 'bonus' view: because the Moon wobbles, or 'librates,' we eventually see 59% of its surface over time. Even the 'Full Moon' is a technicality, appearing 100% illuminated for only a moment when perfectly opposite the Sun.
angle: The Moon’s phases aren't caused by Earth's shadow, but by the Moon's shadow on its own surface.
disputed: S5 claims the Moon is technically never 100 percent full because of its orbital tilt, while S1 and S6 describe it as a standard major phase; the script should explain it as a momentary alignment.
S5 refers to the orbital tilt as 5 percent while S1 and S6 define it as 5 degrees; the script should use 5 degrees as the scientific standard.
S6 emphasizes there is no permanently dark side of the Moon, while common myths assume otherwise; the script should use the fact that half is always lit to debunk the 'dark side' concept.
